newsitem.title: THAILAND: Analysts split on any Thai downgrade by Moody's.
newsitem.headline: Analysts split on any Thai downgrade by Moody's.

text.p: Analysts were divided on whether Moody's Investor Service would downgrade Thailand's debt rating as the rating agency's representatives met top government officials on Wednesday.
Some said a downgrade by the rating agency was likely given the country's beleagured finance sector, slowing economic growth and a big current account deficit.
But others disagreed and said the pessimism over the Thai economy might have been blown out of proportion and that its economic fundamentals were improving.
"I think the chance (of a credit downgrade) is pretty high, given all the trouble Thailand is facing at the moment," said an economist at an European bank who declined to be identified.

"It will be a bit tough for the country to convince Moody's that the economy is in sound condition, that interest rates are in the right direction, and that the problems in the finance sector will be contained," he added.

Moody's officials met Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan and central bank officials on Wednesday for discussions on key economic concerns. They plan to meet a government panel of economic officials for mored detailed talks on Thursday.

Concerns that have plagued the country recently include the status of the weak Thai baht, which has come in for speculative attack, the central bank's high interest rate policy, and the soundness of the troubled finance and property sectors.
Moody's announced in February that it had put Thailand's long-term credit rating under review for a possible downgrade.

It said the review of the country's A-2 rating for long-term sovereign credit was prompted by concerns about the build-up of short-term foreign debt, financial institutions' exposure to the troubled property sector and the rise of non-performing loans.
A senior central bank official told reporters he expected a decision from Moodys in the next one or two months.
Any Moody's downgrade would raise the cost of funds for Thai borrowers and erode investor confidence, analysts said. Late last year Moody's downgraded Thailand's short-term debt rating.
Standard and Poor's, the other international rating agency, has said it has no plans to downgrade Thailand.

Earlier this week, Thai authorities ordered a shake-up of the ailing finance sector and told 10 finance firms to raise their capital after liquidity problems. Banks and finance firms were asked to raise provisions for bad loans, mainly granted to the troubled property sector.

"Even though they (government) have launched stiff measures, it won't mean anything if they can't convince the agency clearly that these measures will be successfully implemented," said Kanchit Assavasamrarn of Vickers Ballas.
Wong Yit Fan, chief regional economist of Standard Chartered, said any downgrade of Thailand was not justified.
"I've seen financial crises. I've seen banks in trouble and those problems are in Thailand, but they are not so severe as to derail the economy," he told Reuters.
He believed non-performing loans were higher than 7.73 percent of total credit established by the central bank, but nevertheless saw the problems as manageable.
"A lot of people are worried about non-performing loans in the finance sector... But compared to others in the region, Thailand's non-performing loans are still okay.
"Compare that with Malaysia. In 1988, the country had 33 percent of non-performing loans," he added.
